\chapter{Somebody Else}
\label{ch:bn-somebody-else}
\hlchaptermodality{34}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can talk about a third person, choose the respectful form when I should, sort them by how far away they are, and say what is theirs.}

The third person arrives — graded for respect on the same ladder as \bn{তুমি} and \bn{আপনি}, and sorted by distance on the same heads as \bn{এই} and \bn{ওই} — and with it the possessive column reaches its third of six cells.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[she]{\bn{সে} (she) — he, she}

\label{lesson:BN-C23-she}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{I}. Say the two words for \textbf{you}, and say which one is for somebody you are careful with.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the word that points at something near — \emph{ei}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{সে}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{সে} \bn{ভালো}} — \emph{she bhālo} — \textbf{he is well}, or \textbf{she is well.}
\end{quote}

Thirty-three chapters, and every sentence this book can build has been about \textbf{\bn{আমি}} or \textbf{\bn{তুমি}}. Somebody is either speaking or being spoken to. Nobody has ever been \textbf{talked about}.

\textbf{\bn{সে}} is the word that changes that, and it does two things at once that English needs two words for. It is \emph{he} and it is \emph{she}, and Bengali will not tell you which. Sex is not marked on a Bengali pronoun at all — not here, not anywhere.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the third row of a table you already half know}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{plain} & \textbf{careful} \\
\midrule
I & \textbf{\bn{আমি}} & — \\
you & \textbf{\bn{তুমি}} & \textbf{\bn{আপনি}} \\
he, she & \textbf{\bn{সে}} & \emph{next lesson} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Chapter two taught you that Bengali grades \textbf{you} for respect. It grades the third person the same way, on the same ladder, and the careful form arrives in the next lesson. What the table shows is that \textbf{\bn{সে}} is the \emph{plain} one: it is what you use of a child, a friend, a younger sibling — and what you must not use of somebody's grandmother.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{she bhālo}
  \item the three persons in a row — \emph{āmi}, \emph{tumi}, \emph{she}
  \item pointing and then naming — \emph{ei bhāiṭi} … \emph{she bhālo}
  \item it covers both — \emph{she} for a brother, \emph{she} for a sister
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \textbf{\bn{সে}} mean \emph{he} or \emph{she}? (\textbf{Both} — Bengali does not mark it.) Which rung of the respect ladder is it on? (\textbf{The plain one}, like \textbf{\bn{তুমি}}.) And what could this book not do before this word? (\textbf{Talk about anybody} who was not speaking or being spoken to.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tini]{\bn{তিনি} (tini) — he, she, respectfully}

\label{lesson:BN-C23-tini}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{he is well} with the plain pronoun. Then say the careful word for \textbf{you}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{তিনি}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{তিনি} \bn{ভালো}} — \emph{tini bhālo} — \textbf{he is well}, said of somebody you respect.
\end{quote}

The table from the last lesson is now complete:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{plain} & \textbf{careful} \\
\midrule
I & \textbf{\bn{আমি}} & — \\
you & \textbf{\bn{তুমি}} & \textbf{\bn{আপনি}} \\
he, she & \textbf{\bn{সে}} & \textbf{\bn{তিনি}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two rungs in the second person, two rungs in the third, and the choice is made the same way both times: age, standing, and how well you know them.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the cost of getting it wrong}]
This is not a nicety a learner can put off. Bengali offers no neutral pronoun to hide behind: every time you mention a third person you have to pick a rung, and picking the low one about somebody's elder is a real discourtesy — the kind you would then be apologising for with \emph{dukkhito}.

The safe habit while you are learning: \textbf{\bn{তিনি}} for anybody older than you or unknown to you, \textbf{\bn{সে}} for children and for friends your own age. Over-politeness is heard as slightly formal. Under-politeness is heard as rude.

Notice too that \textbf{\bn{তিনি}} and \textbf{\bn{আপনি}} share their ending. The careful rung is built the same way on both rows, which is one shape to learn rather than two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tini bhālo}
  \item the two rungs, back to back — \emph{she bhālo}, \emph{tini bhālo}
  \item all four pronouns — \emph{tumi}, \emph{āpni}, \emph{she}, \emph{tini}
  \item of an elder brother, carefully — \emph{ei bhāiṭi} … \emph{tini bhālo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which second-person word does \textbf{\bn{তিনি}} match? (\textbf{\bn{আপনি}} — same rung, same ending.) Can a Bengali speaker avoid the choice? (\textbf{No} — there is no neutral third-person pronoun.) And which one do you use of somebody older than you? (\textbf{\bn{তিনি}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[o]{\bn{ও} (o) — him, her, the one standing there}

\label{lesson:BN-C23-o-pron}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{that shirt}. Then say what \textbf{\bn{ও}} does when it stands between two things.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{ও} as a person}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{ও} \bn{ভালো}} — \emph{o bhālo} — \textbf{he is well} — said of somebody standing right there.
\end{quote}

Chapter thirty-two promised this letter a third job, and here it is. \textbf{\bn{ও}} on its own, in front of a verb, is a \textbf{person}: the one nearby, the one you could gesture at.

Three jobs, one syllable, and they are told apart by position:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{where it sits} & \textbf{what it is} \\
\midrule
between two things & \textbf{also, and} \\
in front of a noun, as \textbf{\bn{ওই}} & \textbf{that} \\
standing alone as a subject & \textbf{him, her} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: near, there, and away}]
Bengali's third person is not one word but a small set sorted by \textbf{how far away the person is}, exactly the way its pointing words are:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\bn{এ}} — this one, right here
  \item \textbf{\bn{ও}} — that one, over there
  \item \textbf{\bn{সে}} — him, her, away from us both, or not present at all
\end{itemize}

They are all the plain rung. \textbf{\bn{তিনি}} is the careful rung for all three distances at once, which is why it has no near-and-far partners.

So the pointing system you built two chapters ago was never only about shirts. It sorts people too, and that is why \textbf{\bn{এই}} and \textbf{\bn{ওই}} were worth a whole chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{o bhālo}
  \item the three distances — \emph{e}, \emph{o}, \emph{she}
  \item the three jobs of one syllable — \emph{bhāi o bôn}; \emph{oi jāmā}; \emph{o bhālo}
  \item the careful rung, which covers all three — \emph{tini bhālo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the three jobs of \textbf{\bn{ও}}, and what tells them apart? (\textbf{Also}, \textbf{that}, \textbf{him or her} — told apart by \textbf{where it sits}.) Which of the plain third-person words is for somebody not present? (\textbf{\bn{সে}}.) And how many careful forms are there? (\textbf{One} — \textbf{\bn{তিনি}} covers every distance.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tār]{\bn{তার} (tār) — his, her}

\label{lesson:BN-C23-tar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{my}. Then say \textbf{he is well}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{তার}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{তার} \bn{ভাই}} — \emph{tār bhāi} — \textbf{his brother}, or \textbf{her brother.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{তার} \bn{জামাটা}} — \emph{tār jāmāṭā} — \textbf{his shirt} (that one).
\end{quote}

Chapter two taught \textbf{\bn{আমার}} and \textbf{\bn{তোমার}} and left it there, so possession has been available for exactly two people out of everybody in the world. \textbf{\bn{তার}} is the third, and it is built the way the other two are:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{pronoun} & \textbf{possessive} \\
\midrule
I & \textbf{\bn{আমি}} & \textbf{\bn{আমার}} \\
you & \textbf{\bn{তুমি}} & \textbf{\bn{তোমার}} \\
he, she & \textbf{\bn{সে}} & \textbf{\bn{তার}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

An \textbf{-\bn{র}} on the end, every time. That is not a coincidence to be memorised: it is a \textbf{case ending}, the same kind of stuck-on piece as the classifier, and it is the second of several you will meet.

The careful form follows the same rule from \textbf{\bn{তিনি}}: \textbf{\bn{তাঁর}} — \emph{tā̃r} — with the moon-dot you learned in chapter five sitting over the vowel.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: order does not change}]
A possessive takes the front slot, in front of everything, and the noun keeps its own ending at the back exactly as before:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{তার} \bn{লাল} \bn{জামাটা}} — \emph{tār lāl jāmāṭā} — \textbf{his red shirt.}
\end{quote}

Front to back: \textbf{whose}, then \textbf{what kind}, then \textbf{the thing} with its ending. Nothing you learned about the queue has changed; one more slot has been filled at its head.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tār bhāi}
  \item the three possessives in a row — \emph{āmār}, \emph{tomār}, \emph{tār}
  \item the careful one — \emph{tā̃r bhāi}
  \item the full queue — \emph{tār lāl jāmāṭā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What ending turns a Bengali pronoun into a possessive? (\textbf{-\bn{র}}.) Which pronoun is \textbf{\bn{তার}} built on? (\textbf{\bn{সে}}.) And where in the phrase does a possessive stand? (\textbf{At the front}, before everything.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[she · tini · o · tār]{Somebody else}

\label{lesson:BN-R23-somebody-else}



\begin{quote}
Three plain third-person words arrived in this chapter, sorted by distance, and one careful word that covers all three. Name them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{she bhālo}, \emph{tini bhālo}, \emph{o bhālo}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tār bhāi}, then the careful \emph{tā̃r bhāi}
  \item \emph{Say it:} and the denial — \emph{she bhālo nôy}
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the ending that pluralises a living noun — \emph{-rā}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — the whole family, talked about}
Until this chapter every sentence in this book was about the speaker or the listener. The family of chapter twenty-one has been sitting in the book for a hundred lessons and could never once be the subject of a sentence. Take them cold.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the six persons in order — \emph{āmi}, \emph{tumi}, \emph{āpni}, \emph{she}, \emph{tini}, \emph{o}
  \item the three possessives — \emph{āmār}, \emph{tomār}, \emph{tār}
  \item a brother, pointed at and then talked about — \emph{ei bhāiṭi} … \emph{tini bhālo}
  \item a friend, plainly — \emph{oi bôndhuṭā} … \emph{she bhālo}
  \item whose face — \emph{tār mukhṭā}
  \item his family, and his brothers — \emph{tār pôribārṭā}, \emph{tār bhāirā}
  \item whose shirt, with everything in the queue — \emph{tār lāl jāmāṭā}
  \item the three jobs of one syllable, once more — \emph{bhāi o bôn}; \emph{oi jāmā}; \emph{o bhālo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does Bengali mark \emph{he} against \emph{she}? (\textbf{No.}) How many rungs of respect does the third person have? (\textbf{Two} — \textbf{\bn{সে}} and \textbf{\bn{তিনি}}.) What sorts \textbf{\bn{এ}}, \textbf{\bn{ও}} and \textbf{\bn{সে}} from each other? (\textbf{How far away the person is}.) And what ending makes a possessive? (\textbf{-\bn{র}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
